</div>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 9pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">adjusted tangible assets; a &#x201C;Tier&nbsp;I risk-based capital&#x201D; ratio&nbsp;&#x2014; an institution&#x2019;s adjusted Tier&nbsp;I capital as a percentage of total risk-weighted assets; a &#x201C;total risk-based capital&#x201D; ratio&nbsp;&#x2014; the percentage of total risk-based capital to total risk-weighted assets; and a &#x201C;tangible equity&#x201D; ratio&nbsp;&#x2014; the ratio of tangible capital to total tangible assets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Federal statutes and OCC regulations have established five capital categories for federal savings banks:&nbsp;&nbsp;well-capitalized, adequately capitalized, undercapitalized, significantly undercapitalized and critically undercapitalized.&nbsp;&nbsp;The federal banking agencies have jointly specified by regulation the relevant capital level for each category.&nbsp;&nbsp;An institution is defined as well-capitalized when its total risk-based capital ratio is at least 10.00%, its Tier I risk-based capital ratio is at least 6.00%, its Tier I (core) capital ratio is at least 5.00%, and it is not subject to any federal supervisory order or directive to meet a specific capital level.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As of June 30, 2013, </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">the Bank was deemed to be &#x201C;well capitalized,&#x201D; without giving effect to the final Basel III capital rules.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;See also </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Note 18</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> in the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2013, June 29, 2012 and June 24, 2011 included under Item 8. &#x201C;Financial Statements and </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Supplementary Data.&#x201D;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">In December 2010, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (the &#x201C;Basel Committee&#x201D;) released a revised final framework for the regulation of capital and liquidity of internationally active banking organizations. These new frameworks are generally referred to as &#x201C;Basel III&#x201D;.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">In July 2013, the OCC and FRB approved their final rule that implements the Basel III regulatory capital reform and certain changes required by the Dodd-Frank Act in the United States.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the final rule, minimum requirements will increase for both the quantity and quality of capital held by banking organizations, including the company and the Bank.&nbsp;&nbsp;To be well capitalized for purposes of the prompt correction action levels of the Basel III final rule, an insured depository institution must maintain a total risk-based capital ratio of 10% or more; a tier 1 capital ratio of 8% or more; a common equity tier 1 capital ratio of 6.5% or more; and a leverage ratio of 5% or more.&nbsp;&nbsp;An adequately-capitalized depository institution must maintain a total risk-based capital ratio of 8% or more; a tier 1 capital ratio of 6% or more; a common equity tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5% or more; and a leverage ratio of 4% or more.&nbsp;&nbsp;An insured depository institution is undercapitalized under the final rule if its total capital ratio is less than 8%, if its tier 1 capital ratio is less than 6%, its common equity tier 1 capital ratio is less than 4.5%, or its leverage ratio is less than 4%.&nbsp;&nbsp;If an institution&#x2019;s tier 1 capital ratio is less than 4%, or its common equity tier 1 capital ratio is less than 3%, it would be considered significantly undercapitalized. The other numerical capital ratio thresholds for being significantly undercapitalized are the same as </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">the current rules.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Under the Basel III final rule, the new common equity tier 1 capital</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> to risk-weighted assets ratio, the Tier I capital ratio and the total capital ratio will also have a capital conservation buffer of 2.5% of risk-weighted assets that will phase in beginning on January 1, 2016 though January 1, 2018.&nbsp;&nbsp;An institution will be subject to limitations on paying dividends, engaging in share repurchases, and paying discretionary bonuses if its capital level falls below the buffer amount.</font><font style="display: inline;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">On the quality of capital side, the Basel III final rule emphasizes common equity tier 1 capital, the most loss-absorbing form of capital, and implements strict eligibility criteria for regulatory capital instruments.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Basel III final rule also improves the methodology for calculating risk-weighted assets to enhance risk sensitivity.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The effective date for this new capital framework for us is January 1, 2015.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Under the Basel III final rule, the Bank will now calculate tangible equity based on average total assets rather than period-end total assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;Bank regulators are required to take &#x201C;prompt corrective action&#x201D;, or PCA, to resolve problems associated with insured depository institutions whose capital declines below certain levels.&nbsp;&nbsp;Federal banking agencies are required to take various mandatory supervisory actions and are authorized to take other discretionary actions with respect to institutions that are &#x201C;undercapitalized,&#x201D; &#x201C;significantly undercapitalized&#x201D; or &#x201C;critically undercapitalized.&#x201D;&nbsp;&nbsp;The severity of the action depends upon the capital category in which the institution is placed.&nbsp;&nbsp;The new capital conservation buffer is designed to absorb losses in stressful periods and the banking agencies believe that it is appropriate for a depository institution to be able to use some of its capital conservation buffer without being considered less than well capitalized for PCA purposes.&nbsp;&nbsp;Generally, subject to a narrow </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">exception, the banking regulator must appoint a receiver or conservator for an institution that is critically undercapitalized.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">In the</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> event an institution becomes &#x201C;undercapitalized,&#x201D; it must submit an acceptable capital restoration plan to the appropriate regulator.&nbsp;&nbsp;The capital restoration plan will not be accepted by the regulators unless, among other requirements, each company having control of the undercapitalized institution guarantees the subsidiary&#x2019;s compliance with the capital restoration plan up to a certain specified amount.&nbsp;&nbsp;Any such guarantee from a depository institution&#x2019;s holding company is entitled to a priority of payment in bankruptcy.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The aggregate liability of the holding company of an undercapitalized depository institution is limited to the lesser of 5% of the institution&#x2019;s assets at the time it became undercapitalized or the amount necessary to cause the institution to be &#x201C;adequately capitalized.&#x201D;&nbsp;&nbsp;The bank regulators have greater power in situations where an institution becomes &#x201C;significantly&#x201D; or &#x201C;critically&#x201D; undercapitalized or fails to submit a capital restoration plan.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, the guarantee can be limited for a holding company that is a &#x201C;functionally regulated affiliate&#x201D; of the depository institution, such as a holding company that is a broker/dealer registered with the SEC, if the functional regulator of the affiliate objects.&nbsp;&nbsp;For example, the FRB could require an SEC registered broker/dealer holding company for an undercapitalized federal savings bank to guarantee the bank&#x2019;s capital </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">restoration plan, subject to the limitations summarized above and subject to an objection from the holding company&#x2019;s functional regulator, the SEC.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">An undercapitalized institution is also generally prohibited from increasing its average total assets, making acquisitions, establishing branches or engaging in any new line of business, except under an accepted capital restoration plan or with FDIC approval.&nbsp;&nbsp;The prompt corrective action regulations also establish procedures for downgrading an institution to a lower capital category based on supervisory factors other than capital.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The FDIC insures the deposits of the Bank up to the applicable maximum in each account, or up to $250,000 per account. FDIC deposit insurance is backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">All FDIC insured institutions are required to pay assessments to the FDIC based on their average assets.&nbsp; In fiscal 2012, the Bank paid an assessment rate of 23 basis points.&nbsp; Due to continued improvement in the credit quality of the Bank&#x2019;s loan portfolio, the FDIC assessment rate was decreased to 14 basis points in the second half of fiscal 2013.&nbsp; &nbsp;The Bank believes that this change will result in significant FDIC insurance costs savings.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">All FDIC insured institutions are required to pay additional assessments to the FDIC at an annual rate of approximately 0.64 basis points of average assets to fund interest payments on bonds issued by the Financing Corporation, an agency of the federal government established to recapitalize the predecessor to the Savings Association Insurance Fund.&nbsp;&nbsp;These assessments will continue until the Financing Corporation bonds mature in 2017 through 2019.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Under the Dodd-Frank Act, the FDIC was given much greater discretion to manage the DIF, including where to set the designated reserve ratio (&#x201C;DRR&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;The Dodd-Frank Act increased the DRR from 1.15 percent to 1.35 percent and left unchanged the requirement that the FDIC Board set the DRR annually.&nbsp;&nbsp;The FDIC Board must set the DRR according to the following factors:&nbsp;&nbsp;(i) risk of loss to the insurance fund; (ii) economic conditions affecting the banking industry; (iii) preventing sharp swings in the assessment rates and (iv) any other factors it deems important.&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on those factors, the FDIC Board decided to set the DRR at 2.00 percent based on a historical analysis of losses to the DIF.&nbsp;&nbsp;The analysis showed in order to maintain a positive fund balance and steady, predictable assessment rates, the DRR must be at least 2.00 percent as a long-term, minimum goal.&nbsp;&nbsp;The DRR increase may increase FDIC deposit insurance assessments in the future.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:18pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Numerous regulations promulgated by the federal banking agencies, including the Bureau, as amended from time to time, affect the business operations of the Bank. These include regulations relating to holding company regulation, equal credit opportunity, electronic fund transfers, fair credit reporting, fair debt collection, service members civil relief, collection of checks, insider lending, lending limits, truth in lending, truth in savings, home ownership and equity protection, transactions with affiliates and availability of funds. Under FRB regulations, the Bank is required to maintain a reserve against its transaction accounts (primarily interest-bearing and noninterest-bearing checking accounts). Because reserves must generally be maintained in cash or in noninterest-bearing accounts, the historical effect of the reserve requirements is to increase the Bank&#x2019;s cost of funds. The Federal Reserve banks are authorized to pay interest on reserves, subject to regulations of the FRB, effective October 1, 2008. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Bank is subject to regulation by the Bureau, established by the Dodd-Frank Act as an independent entity within the Federal Reserve, which has the authority to promulgate consumer protection regulations applicable to all entities offering consumer financial services or products, including banks. The Bureau has broad rule-making authority for a wide range of consumer protection laws, including but not limited to, laws relating to alternative mortgage transaction parity, consumer leasing, electronic fund transfers, equal credit opportunity, fair credit billing, fair credit reporting, home owners protection, fair debt collection practices, lack of deposit insurance, consumer financial privacy, home mortgage disclosure, home ownership and equity protection, real estate settlement procedures, mortgage licensing, truth in lending and truth in savings, among other laws.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bureau also has the authority to prohibit &#x201C;unfair, deceptive or abusive&#x201D; acts and practices related to offering consumer financial services or products.&nbsp;&nbsp;Because the Bank has less than $10 billion in total assets, the primary federal regulator with examination authority over the Bank for compliance with consumer financial protection laws is the OCC.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:10.8pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:18pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (&#x201C;GLBA&#x201D;) includes provisions that give consumers protections regarding the transfer and use of their nonpublic personal information by financial institutions. In addition, states are permitted under the GLBA to have their own privacy laws, which may offer greater protection to consumers than the GLBA. Numerous states in which the Bank does business have enacted such laws.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:10.8pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:18pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Bank Secrecy Act, the PATRIOT Act and rules and regulation of the Office of Foreign Assets Control (&#x201C;OFAC Rules&#x201D;) include numerous provisions designed to fight international money laundering and to block terrorist access to the U.S.&nbsp;financial system. We have established policies and procedures to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Bank Secrecy Act, the PATRIOT Act and OFAC Rules.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 9pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:18pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 (&#x201C;CRA&#x201D;) requires deposit institutions to assist in meeting the credit needs of their market areas consistent with safe and sound banking practice.&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the CRA, each depository institution is required to help meet the credit needs of its market areas by, among other things, providing credit to low- and moderate-income individuals and communities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Depository institutions are periodically examined for compliance with the CRA and are assigned ratings.&nbsp;&nbsp;The primary federal regulatory agency assigns one of four possible ratings to an institution&#x2019;s CRA performance and is required to make public an institution&#x2019;s rating and written evaluation. The four possible ratings of meeting community credit needs are outstanding, satisfactory, needs to improve and substantial non-compliance. In the most recent examination, we received a &#x201C;Satisfactory&#x201D; CRA rating from the OTS.&nbsp;&nbsp;In the future, the OCC will examine the Bank for CRA compliance.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Bank has committed $8.0 million to three investments in limited partnership equity funds as a cost effective way of meeting its obligations under the CRA.&nbsp;&nbsp;As of June 30, 2013, the Bank had invested $180,000 of its aggregate commitment to the three funds.&nbsp;&nbsp;These investments are subject to the Volcker Rule provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act, which limits the Bank&#x2019;s ownership interest to 3% in any private equity fund.&nbsp;&nbsp;The federal agencies that will enforce the Volcker Rule have stated&nbsp;&nbsp;that it will become effective July 21, 2014.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;After the Volcker Rule becomes effective, financial institutions can request up to three additional one year extensions from the FRB, and the FRB can grant up to a five year extension for investments in illiquid funds made on or before May 21, 2010, and funds that are &#x201C;designed primarily to promote the public welfare&#x201D; are not subject to the rule as proposed.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank&#x2019;s ownership percentage in two of the limited partnership equity funds are greater than 3% and would qualify as illiquid funds.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, these limited partnership equity funds may qualify as &#x201C;designed primarily to promote the public welfare&#x201D; as the Bank invests in these funds as a cost effective way of meeting its obligations under the CRA.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank&#x2019;s ownership percentage in the other limited partnership equity fund is less than 3%. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Transactions between the Bank and its nonbanking affiliates, including us, are subject to Section 23A of the Federal Reserve Act.&nbsp;&nbsp;In general, Section 23A imposes limits on the amount of such transactions, and also requires certain levels of collateral for loans to affiliated parties.&nbsp;&nbsp;Affiliate transactions are also subject to Section 23B of the Federal Reserve Act, which generally requires that certain transactions between the Bank and its affiliates be on substantially the same terms, or at least terms as favorable to the Bank, as those prevailing at the time for comparable transactions with or involving other nonaffiliated persons.&nbsp;&nbsp;The FRB&#x2019;s Regulation W implements Section 23A and 23B of the Federal Reserve Act and codifies prior interpretive guidance with respect to affiliate transactions.&nbsp;&nbsp;On July 21, 2011, an amendment made in the Dodd-Frank Act became effective to amend the definition of &#x201C;affiliate&#x201D; in Section 23A of the Federal Reserve Act to include &#x201C;any investment fund with respect to which a member bank or an affiliate thereof is an investment advisor.&#x201D; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The restrictions on loans to directors, executive officers, principal stockholders and their related interests (collectively referred to herein as &#x201C;insiders&#x201D;) contained in the Federal Reserve Act and Regulation O apply to all insured depository institutions, their subsidiaries and holding companies.&nbsp;&nbsp;These restrictions include limits on loans to one borrower and conditions that must be met before such a loan can be made.&nbsp;&nbsp;There is also an aggregate limitation on all loans to insiders and their related interests.&nbsp;&nbsp;These loans cannot exceed the institution&#x2019;s total unimpaired capital and surplus, and the OCC may determine that a lesser amount is appropriate.&nbsp;&nbsp;Insiders are subject to enforcement actions for knowingly accepting loans in violation of applicable restrictions.&nbsp;&nbsp;On July 21, 2011, an amendment made in the Dodd-Frank Act became effective to amend the statutes placing limitations on loans to insiders by including credit exposures to the person arising from a derivatives transaction, repurchase agreement, reverse repurchase agreement, securities lending transaction or securities borrowing transaction between the member bank and the person within the definition of an extension of credit to an insider. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Subject to various exceptions, savings and loan holding companies and their affiliates are generally prohibited from tying the provision of certain services, such as extensions of credit, to certain other services offered by a holding company or its affiliates.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We are subject to the requirements of the Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act of 2008,(the &#x201C;SAFE Act&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;The SAFE Act requires mortgage loan originators who are employees of regulated institutions (including banks and certain of their subsidiaries) to be registered with the Nationwide Mortgage Licensing System and Registry (the &#x201C;Registry&#x201D;), a database established by the Conference of State Bank Supervisors and the American Association of Residential Mortgage Regulators to support the licensing of mortgage loan originators by each state.&nbsp;&nbsp;As part of this registration process, mortgage loan originators must furnish the Registry with background information and fingerprints for a background check.&nbsp;&nbsp;The SAFE Act generally prohibits employees of a regulated financial institution from originating residential mortgage loans without first registering with the Registry and maintaining that registration.&nbsp;&nbsp;Financial institutions must also adopt policies and procedures to ensure compliance with the SAFE Act.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:10.8pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">

The FDIC may increase or decrease the assessment rate schedule on a semi-annual basis.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt 6pt;text-align:left;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Our business, reputation, financial condition, operating results and cash flows can be impacted by a number of factors.&nbsp;&nbsp;Many of these factors are beyond our control and may significantly impact us during periods of market volatility or reduced liquidity.&nbsp;&nbsp;The potential harm from any one of these risks, or others, could cause our actual results to vary materially from recent results or from anticipated future results.&nbsp;&nbsp;Some risks may adversely impact not only our own operations, but the banking or securities industry in general which could also produce marked swings in the trading price of our securities.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Although the risks </font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 10pt">

</div>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt 6pt;text-align:left;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">described below are those that management believes are the most significant, these are not the only risks facing our company.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additional risks and uncertainties not currently known to us or that we currently do not deem to be material may also materially affect our business, reputation, financial condition, operating results and cash flows.&nbsp;&nbsp;We may amend or supplement these risk factors from time to time in the reports we file with the SEC.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">RISKS SPECIFIC TO OUR INDUSTRIES</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Compliance with regulatory reform legislation may increase our costs and limit our ability to pursue business opportunities.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">On July 21, 2010, the President of the United States signed into law the Dodd-Frank Act. The full impact of the Dodd-Frank Act and its implementing regulations on the financial services industry in general, and on us in particular, is still uncertain. SWS Group and the Bank will be subject to additional significant regulatory requirements, which may have a material impact on each or both of them, or SWS as a whole. The principal effects of the Dodd-Frank Act on our business include:</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<div style="width:100%"><table style="" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0"><tr><td align="left" valign="top" style="width: 50.00pt; display: inline;">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
				<font style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 32pt;font-family:Symbol;font-size:9pt;"> &#xB7;</font>
			</p>
		</td><td align="left" valign="top">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">changes to the supervisory structure for SWS Group and the Bank;</font></p></td></tr></table></div>
		<div style="width:100%"><table style="" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0"><tr><td align="left" valign="top" style="width: 50.00pt; display: inline;">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
				<font style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 32pt;font-family:Symbol;font-size:9pt;"> &#xB7;</font>
			</p>
		</td><td align="left" valign="top">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">changes to regulatory capital requirements applicable to SWS Group and the Bank;</font></p></td></tr></table></div>
		<div style="width:100%"><table style="" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0"><tr><td align="left" valign="top" style="width: 50.00pt; display: inline;">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
				<font style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 32pt;font-family:Symbol;font-size:9pt;"> &#xB7;</font>
			</p>
		</td><td align="left" valign="top">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">establishment of&nbsp;&nbsp;the Bureau with broad authority to implement new consumer protection regulations; </font></p></td></tr></table></div>
		<div style="width:100%"><table style="" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0"><tr><td align="left" valign="top" style="width: 50.00pt; display: inline;">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
				<font style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 32pt;font-family:Symbol;font-size:9pt;"> &#xB7;</font>
			</p>
		</td><td align="left" valign="top">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">increases in the minimum reserve ratio for the deposit insurance fund of the FDIC to 2.00% and a change in the base for FDIC insurance assessments; and</font></p></td></tr></table></div>
		<div style="width:100%"><table style="" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0"><tr><td align="left" valign="top" style="width: 50.00pt; display: inline;">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
				<font style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 32pt;font-family:Symbol;font-size:9pt;"> &#xB7;</font>
			</p>
		</td><td align="left" valign="top">
			<p style="font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">proposed prohibitions on &#x201C;proprietary trading&#x201D; and proposed limitations with respect to the sponsorship of, and investment in, hedge funds and private equity under the Volcker Rule.</font></p></td></tr></table></div>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:32.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">As a result of the Dodd-Frank Act, the OTS was abolished and, on July 21, 2011, the </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">OCC</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> took over supervision and regulation of federal thrifts, such as the Bank, and the FRB took over supervision and regulation of savings and loan holding companies, including SWS Group. As a result, we will be subject to the regulatory capital and activity requirements, including the new Basel III regulatory capital framework approved by the FRB in July 2013. The Dodd-Frank Act also requires that SWS Group serve as a &#x201C;source of strength&#x201D; for the Bank.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:32.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Dodd-Frank Act created a new independent regulatory body, the Bureau, which was given broad rulemaking authority to implement the consumer protection laws that apply to banks and thrifts and to prohibit &#x201C;unfair, deceptive or abusive&#x201D; acts and practices. The Dodd-Frank Act permits states to adopt consumer protection laws and regulations that are stricter than those regulations promulgated by this new independent regulatory body.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:32.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We are closely monitoring regulatory developments related to the Volcker Rule.&nbsp;&nbsp;Until the final regulations under the Volcker Rule are adopted, the precise definition of prohibited &#x201C;proprietary trading&#x201D;, the scope of any exceptions for market making and hedging, and the scope of permitted hedge fund and private equity fund investments remains uncertain.&nbsp;&nbsp;It is unclear under the proposed rules whether some portion of our market-making and risk mitigation activities that are currently conducted will be required to be curtailed or will be otherwise adversely affected.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, the proposed rules would prohibit certain securitization structures and would prohibit U.S. banking entities from sponsoring or investing in certain non-U.S. funds.&nbsp;&nbsp;Also, with respect to certain of our investments in illiquid private equity funds, if regulators do not exercise their authority to permit us to hold such investments beyond the minimum statutory divestment period, we could incur substantial losses when we dispose of such investments, as we may be forced to sell such investments at a substantial discount in the secondary market as a result of both the constrained timing of such sales and the possibility that other financial institutions are liquidating their investments at the same time.&nbsp;&nbsp;When the final regulations are promulgated, we will make plans to implement compliance with the Volcker Rule.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:32.4pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Full implementation of the Dodd-Frank Act will require many new rules to be issued by numerous federal regulatory agencies over the next several years. Given the significance of the changes and the additional regulatory action required for many of the new provisions, we cannot predict all of the ways or the degree to which our business, financial condition and results of operations may be affected by the Dodd-Frank Act once it is fully implemented. We expect, at a minimum, that our compliance costs will increase.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">We may be adversely affected by increased governmental and regulatory scrutiny or negative publicity.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;Governmental and regulatory scrutiny from regulators, legislative bodies and law enforcement agencies with respect to matters relating to compensation, our business practices, our past actions and other matters has increased dramatically in the past several years.&nbsp;&nbsp;The financial crisis and the current political and public sentiment regarding financial institutions has resulted in a significant amount of adverse press coverage, as well as adverse statements or charges by regulators or other government officials.&nbsp;&nbsp;Press coverage and other public statements that assert some form of wrongdoing often result in some type of investigation by regulators, legislators and law enforcement officials or in lawsuits.&nbsp;&nbsp;Responding to these investigations and lawsuits, regardless of the ultimate outcome of the proceeding, is time consuming and expensive and can divert the time and effort of our senior management from our business. Penalties and fines sought by regulatory authorities have increased substantially over the last several years, and certain regulators have been more likely in recent years to commence enforcement </font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">The impact of the changing regulatory capital requirements and new capital rules are uncertain.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">In July 2013, the OCC and FRB approved a final rule that will substantially amend the risk-based capital rules applicable to SWS Group and the Bank. The final rule implements the &#x201C;Basel III&#x201D; regulatory capital reforms and changes required by the Dodd-Frank Act. The final rule includes new minimum risk-based capital and leverage ratios, which will be effective for SWS Group and the Bank on January 1, 2015, and refines the definition of what constitutes &#x201C;capital&#x201D; for purposes of calculating these ratios. The new minimum capital requirements will be: (i) a new common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5%; (ii) a Tier 1 to risk-based assets capital ratio of 6% (increased from 4%); (iii) a total capital ratio of 8% (unchanged from current rules); and (iv) a Tier 1 leverage ratio of 4%. The final rule also establishes a &#x201C;capital conservation buffer&#x201D; of 2.5% above the new regulatory minimum capital ratios and will result in the following minimum ratios: (i) a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 7.0%; (ii) a Tier 1 to risk-based assets capital ratio of 8.5%; and (iii) a total capital ratio of 10.5%. The new capital conservation buffer requirement would be phased in beginning in January 2016 at 0.625% of risk-weighted assets and would increase each year until fully implemented in January 2019.&nbsp;&nbsp;An institution will be subject to limitations on paying dividends, engaging in share repurchases, and paying discretionary bonuses if its capital level falls below the buffer amount. These limitations will establish a maximum percentage of eligible retained income that can be utilized for such actions. The application of more stringent capital requirements for SWS Group and the Bank could, among other things, adversely affect our results of operations and growth, require the raising of additional capital, restrict our ability to pay dividends or repurchase shares and result in regulatory actions if we were to be unable to comply with such requirements.</font>

The financial services industry and the securities markets generally are materially and adversely affected by recessionary or volatile environments which can cause significant declines in the value of nearly all asset classes. Concerns about financial institution profitability and solvency as a result of general market conditions, particularly in the credit markets, may cause our customers and clients to reduce the level of business that they do with us. Declines in asset values, the lack of liquidity, general uncertainty about economic and market activity and a lack of consumer and investor confidence have negatively impacted, and may continue to negatively impact, our business.</font>

Slowing growth, contraction of credit, increasing energy prices, declines in business or investor confidence or risk tolerance, increases in inflation, higher unemployment, outbreaks of hostilities or other geopolitical instability, corporate, political or other scandals that reduce investor confidence in capital markets and natural disasters, among other things, can affect the global financial markets. In addition, economic or political pressures in a country or region may cause local market disruptions and currency devaluations, which may also affect markets generally. In the event of changes in market conditions, such as interest or foreign exchange rates, equity, fixed income, commodity or real estate valuations, liquidity, availability of credit or volatility, our business could be adversely affected. </font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Risk management processes may not fully mitigate exposure to the various risks that we face, including </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">market, liquidity and credit risk.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;We continue to refine our risk management techniques, strategies and assessment methods on an ongoing basis. However, risk management techniques and strategies, both ours and those available to the market generally, may not be fully effective in mitigating our risk exposure in all economic market environments or against all types of risk. For example, we might fail to identify or anticipate particular risks that our systems are capable of identifying, or the systems that we use, and that are used within the industry generally, may not be capable of identifying certain risks. Some of our strategies for managing risk are based upon our use of observed historical market behavior. We apply statistical and other tools to these observations to quantify our risk exposure. Any failures in our risk management techniques and strategies to accurately quantify our risk exposure could limit our ability to manage risks. In addition, any risk management failures could cause our losses to be significantly greater than the historical measures indicate. Further, our quantified modeling does not take all risks into account. As a result, we also take a qualitative approach in reducing our risk.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our qualitative approach to </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">managing those risks could also prove insufficient, exposing us to material unanticipated losses.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Our business is significantly dependent on net interest margins.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;The profitability of our margin and stock lending businesses depends to a great extent on the difference between interest income earned on loans and investments of customer cash balances and the interest expense paid on customer cash balances and borrowings.&nbsp;&nbsp;The earnings and cash flows of the Bank are also dependent upon the difference between interest income earned on interest-earning assets such as loans and securities and interest expense paid on interest-bearing liabilities such as deposits and borrowed funds.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Interest rates are sensitive to many factors that are beyond our control, including general economic conditions and policies of various governmental and regulatory agencies and, in particular, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.&nbsp;&nbsp;Changes in monetary policy, including changes in interest rates, could affect the interest we receive on loans and securities and the amount of interest we pay on deposits and borrowings.&nbsp;&nbsp;Such changes could also affect our ability to originate loans and obtain deposits and the fair value of our financial assets and liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;If the interest rates paid on deposits and other borrowings increase at a faster rate than the interest rates received on loans and other investments, our net interest income, and therefore our earnings, could be adversely affected.&nbsp;&nbsp;Earnings could also be adversely affected if the interest rates received on loans and other investments fall more quickly than the interest rates paid on deposits and other borrowings.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Our net interest margins may decrease based on the mix of assets in the Bank&#x2019;s portfolio and our investment strategy.&nbsp;&nbsp;In recent years, interest rates have declined to levels that have negatively impacted the net interest margin at the Bank and the </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">broker/dealer</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">. Additionally, as we reposition the Bank&#x2019;s balance sheet to include a portfolio of conservative investment securities, the net interest margin on these assets is likely to be less than we have historically earned on our loan portfolio. Our earnings and results of operations could be adversely affected by any reduction in our net interest margin due to our investment policies, returns on investments or market dynamics.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">As part of the Bank&#x2019;s risk mitigation strategy to reduce its exposure to variability in interest payments on the Bank&#x2019;s variable rate deposits, forward-start interest rate swaps designated as cash flow hedging instruments have been utilized.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank&#x2019;s forward-start interest rate swaps exchange fixed for variable interest payments beginning at a pre-specified date in the future according to the terms the swap agreements.&nbsp;&nbsp;There is no guarantee that the structure of these derivative transactions will operate as designed and remain effective.&nbsp;&nbsp;If these transactions are not effective, our results of operations could be adversely affected.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We may not be able to reduce our operating expenses as a way to reduce operating losses.&nbsp;&nbsp;To the extent our net interest income declines or we face other declines in revenues, we may look to reduce our operating expenses where possible. However, we have limited control over certain costs, and in particular, the cost of meeting regulatory requirements and our cost to access capital or financing, if needed. If we are unable to reduce our operating expenses, our financial condition, results of operations or cash flows could be adversely affected.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Our margin lending, stock lending, securities trading and execution, bank lending and mortgage purchase businesses are all subject to credit risk.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;Credit risk in all areas of our business increases if securities prices decline rapidly because the value of our collateral could fall below the amount of the indebtedness it secures.&nbsp;&nbsp;In rapidly appreciating markets, credit risk increases due to short positions.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our securities lending business as well as our securities trading and execution businesses subject us to credit risk if a counterparty fails to perform or if collateral securing its obligations is insufficient.&nbsp;&nbsp;In securities transactions, we are subject to credit risk during the period between the execution of a trade and the settlement by the customer.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>

The option to convert to self-clearing operations may be attractive due to the fact that as the transaction volume of a broker/dealer grows, the cost of implementing the necessary infrastructure for self-clearing may eventually be offset by the elimination of per transaction processing fees that would otherwise be paid to a clearing firm.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, performing their own clearing services allows self-clearing broker/dealers to retain their customers&#x2019; margin balances, free credit balances and securities for use in margin lending activities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, our correspondents&#x2019; may decide to use the clearing services of one of our competitors or exit the business.&nbsp;&nbsp;Any significant loss of correspondents due to self-clearing or because of their use of a competitor&#x2019;s clearing service could have a material adverse affect on our business, financial condition, results of operations or cash flows.</font>

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:10.5pt;text-align:left;font-family:Times New Roman;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-size: 9pt">

		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">availability of funds from our subsidiaries, including the broker/dealer subsidiaries, which may be subject to restrictions under the net capital rules of the SEC and FINRA, and the Bank, which may be subject to restrictions by federal banking agencies. Specifically, our Credit Agreement with </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Hilltop and Oak Hill limits our quarterly cash dividend to $0.01 per share and only so long as we are not in default of any terms of the Credit Agreement. </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> We currently intend to retain earnings to fund growth and do not plan to pay dividends on our common stock in the near future.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Equity Compensation Plan Information&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Restricted Stock Plan. </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">On November 15, 2012, the stockholders of SWS Group, Inc. approved the adoption of the SWS Group, Inc. 2012 Restricted Stock Plan (&#x201C;2012 Restricted Stock Plan&#x201D;). The 2012 Restricted Stock Plan allows for awards of restricted stock to SWS&#x2019;s directors, officers and employees and authorizes up to 2,630,000 shares of SWS&#x2019;s common stock to be delivered pursuant to awards granted under the 2012 Restricted Stock Plan. The 2012 Restricted Stock Plan expires on November 15, 2022.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">On November 12, 2003, our stockholders </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">approved the adoption of the SWS Group, Inc. 2003 Restricted Stock Plan ("2003 Restricted Stock Plan").&nbsp;&nbsp;In November 2007, the stockholders of SWS Group approved an amendment to the 2003 Restricted Stock Plan to increase the number of shares available hereunder by 500,000 shares.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Restricted Stock Plan allows for awards of up to 1,250,000 shares of our common stock to our directors, officers and employees.&nbsp;&nbsp;No more than 300,000 of the authorized shares may be newly issued shares of common stock.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Restricted Stock Plan terminated on August 21, 2013.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The vesting period for awards under the 2003 Restricted Stock Plan and the 2012 Restricted Stock Plan is determined on an individualized basis by the Compensation Committee of the Board of Directors.&nbsp;&nbsp;In general, restricted stock granted to employees under the restricted stock plans fully vests after three years or is subject to a four year cliff vesting schedule, and restricted stock granted to non-employee directors vests on the first anniversary of the date of grant.&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, the total number of shares outstanding under the 2012 Restricted Stock Plan and the 2003 Restricted Stock Plan was 347,877 and the total number of shares available for future awards was 2,596,305.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Deferred Compensation Plan. </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> On November 10, 2004, the stockholders of SWS Group approved the 2005 Deferred Compensation Plan, the effective date of which was January 1, 2005, for eligible officers and employees to defer a portion of their bonus compensation and commissions.&nbsp;&nbsp;The deferred compensation plan was designed to comply with the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004.&nbsp;&nbsp;Contributions to the deferred compensation plan consist of employee pre-tax contributions and SWS Group&#x2019;s matching contributions, in the form of SWS Group common stock, up to a specified limit. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The assets of the deferred compensation plan include investments in SWS Group&#x2019;s common stock, Westwood Holdings Group, Inc.&#x2019;s ("Westwood") common stock and company-owned life insurance ("COLI").&nbsp;&nbsp;Investments in SWS Group&#x2019;s common stock are carried at cost and are held as treasury stock with an offsetting deferred compensation liability in the equity section of the consolidated statements of financial condition. </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The deferred compensation plan limited the number of shares of SWS Group common stock that may be issued to 375,000 shares.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">On November 17, 2009, the stockholders of SWS Group voted to increase the authorized number of shares of SWS Group common stock available for issuance under the deferred compensation plan from 375,000 shares to 675,000 shares.&nbsp;&nbsp;The number of shares of SWS Group common stock available for future issuance under the plan was 176,679 at June 30, 2013.&nbsp;&nbsp;Investments in Westwood&#x2019;s common stock are carried at market value and recorded as securities available for sale.&nbsp;&nbsp;Investments in COLI are carried at the cash surrender value of the insurance policies and recorded in other assets in the consolidated statements of financial condition.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">For the fiscal year ended June 30, 2013, we had approximately $18.6 million in deferred compensation plan assets, with a market value of $19.4 million.&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, $3.3 million was invested in 301,660 shares of our common stock.&nbsp;&nbsp;Approximately $1.7 million of compensation expense was recorded for participant contributions and employer matching contributions related to the deferred compensation plan in fiscal 2013.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The trustee of the deferred compensation plan is Wilmington Trust Company.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:left;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Stock Option Plans.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;We did not have any active stock option plans at June 30, 2013.&nbsp;&nbsp;All previously issued outstanding options under the SWS Group, Inc. Stock Option Plan (the "1996 Plan") have expired</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;See </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Note 1(u)</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> in the </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2013, June 29, 2012 and June 24, 2011 included under Item 8. &#x201C;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data.&#x201D;</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 10pt"><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font><a name="ManagementsDiscussionandAnalysis"></a><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">ITEM 7. </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;text-transform:uppercase;font-size:9pt;">MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;text-transform:uppercase;font-size:9pt;">CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;text-transform:uppercase;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;text-transform:uppercase;font-size:9pt;">OVERVIEW</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We are engaged in full-service securities brokerage and full-service commercial banking.&nbsp;&nbsp;During the twelve-months ended June 30, 2013, 85% of our total revenues were generated by our full-service brokerage business and 15% of our total revenues were generated by our commercial banking business.&nbsp;&nbsp;While brokerage and banking revenues are dependent upon trading volumes and interest rates, which may fluctuate significantly, a large portion of our expenses remain fixed.&nbsp;&nbsp;Consequently, net operating results can vary significantly from period to period.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Our business is also subject to substantial governmental regulation and changes in legal, regulatory, accounting, tax and compliance requirements, which may have a substantial impact on our business and results of operations.&nbsp;&nbsp;We also face substantial competition in each of our lines of business.&nbsp;&nbsp;See &#x201C;Forward-Looking Statements, &#x201D; Item 1. &#x201C;Business-Competition,&#x201D; Item 1. &#x201C;Business-Regulation&#x201D; and Item 1A. &#x201C;Risk Factors.&#x201D;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We operate through four segments grouped primarily by products, services and customer base:&nbsp;&nbsp;clearing, retail, institutional and banking. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 72pt 5pt 36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Clearing.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We provide clearing and execution services for other broker/dealers (predominantly on a fully disclosed basis).&nbsp;&nbsp;Our clientele includes general securities broker/dealers and firms specializing in high-volume trading.&nbsp;&nbsp;We currently support a wide range of clearing clients, including discount and full-service brokerage firms, direct access firms, registered investment advisors and institutional firms.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition to clearing trades, we tailor our services to meet the specific needs of our clearing correspondents ("correspondents") and offer products and services such as recordkeeping, trade reporting, accounting, general back-office support, securities and margin lending, reorganization assistance and custody of securities.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 72pt 9pt 36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Revenues in this segment are generated primarily through transaction charges to our correspondent firms for clearing their trades.&nbsp;&nbsp;Revenue is also earned from various fees and other processing charges as well as through net interest income on correspondent customer balances.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 72pt 9pt 36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Retail</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We offer retail securities (such as equities, mutual funds and fixed income products), insurance products and managed accounts through the activities of our employee registered representatives and our independent contractors.&nbsp;&nbsp;As a securities broker, we extend margin credit on a secured basis to our retail customers in order to facilitate securities transactions.&nbsp;&nbsp;This segment generates revenue primarily through commissions charged on securities transactions, fees from managed accounts and the sale of insurance products as well as net interest income from retail customer balances.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 72pt 9pt 36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Institutional.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We serve institutional customers in the areas of securities borrowing and lending, public finance, municipal finance, sales and underwriting, investment banking, fixed income sales and equity trading.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our securities borrowing and lending business includes borrowing and lending securities for other broker/dealers, lending institutions, and our own clearing and retail operations.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our municipal finance operations assist public bodies in originating, syndicating and distributing securities of municipalities and political subdivisions.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 28, 2013, we exited the corporate finance business.&nbsp;&nbsp;Future revenues will not include fees from this business. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 72pt 9pt 36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Our fixed income sales and trading group specializes in trading and underwriting U.S. government and government agency bonds, corporate bonds, municipal bonds, mortgage-backed, asset-backed and commercial mortgage-backed securities and structured products.&nbsp;&nbsp;The clients of our fixed income group include corporations, insurance companies, banks, mutual funds, money managers and other institutions.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our equity trading department focuses on executing equity and option orders for clients.&nbsp;&nbsp;We also execute institutional portfolio trades and are a market maker in a limited number of listed securities.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 72pt 9pt 36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Revenues in the institutional segment are derived from the net interest spread on stock loan transactions, commissions, and trading income from fixed income and equity products and investment banking, and underwriting fees from corporate, and municipal securities transactions.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 72pt 9pt 36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Banking</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;We</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> offer traditional banking products and services.&nbsp;&nbsp;We specialize in three primary areas, business banking, focusing on industrial and small business lending, commercial real estate lending&nbsp;&nbsp;and mortgage purchase.&nbsp;&nbsp;We originate the majority of our loans internally, and we believe this business model helps us build more valuable relationships with our customers.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our mortgage purchase division </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Until terminated on January 14, 2013, our banking operations were restricted by and subject to the Order to Cease and Desist, Order No. WN-11-003, effective on February 4, 2011 (the &#x201C;Order&#x201D;) originally issued by the Office of Thrift Supervision and then administered by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (the &#x201C;OCC&#x201D;).&nbsp;&nbsp;On March 16, 2012, the Bank was notified in a letter from the OCC that the OCC allowed relief from certain operating and growth restrictions required under the Order.&nbsp;&nbsp;Specifically, the OCC had no supervisory objection to any future extensions of Small Business Administration (&#x201C;SBA&#x201D;) program 504 loans, commercial real estate owner-occupied loans, or mechanics lien residential 1-4 family construction loans so long as, prior to funding, the Bank&#x2019;s Board of Directors or a designated committee of the Bank approved and certified that it complied with internal policies, accounting principles generally accepted in the United States (&#x201C;GAAP&#x201D;), regulatory guidance, and safe and sound association practices.&nbsp;&nbsp;In connection with the termination of the Order on January 14, 2013, the Bank committed to the OCC that the Bank would, among other things:&nbsp;&nbsp;(i) adhere to the Bank&#x2019;s written business and capital plan as amended from time to time; and (ii) maintain a Tier I capital ratio at least equal to nine percent (9%) of adjusted total assets and a total risk-based capital ratio of at least twelve percent (12%).</font>
