			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;font-size:8pt;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Loans and Allowance for Probable Loan Losses</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:36pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Bank grants loans to customers primarily within Texas and New Mexico.&nbsp;&nbsp;In the ordinary course of business, the Bank also purchases mortgage loans that have been originated in various areas of the United States.&nbsp;&nbsp;Although the Bank has a diversified loan portfolio, a substantial portion of its portfolio is dependent upon the general economic conditions in Texas and New Mexico.&nbsp;&nbsp;Substantially all of the Bank&#x2019;s loans are col</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">lateralized with real estate. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The allowance for loan losses is maintained to absorb management&#x2019;s estimate of probable loan losses inherent in the loan portfolio at each reporting date.&nbsp;&nbsp;The allowance for loan losses is established as losses are estimated to have occurred through a provision for loan losses charged to earnings.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loan losses are charged against the allowance when management determines the collection of principal is remote.&nbsp;&nbsp;Subsequent recoveries are recorded through the allowance.&nbsp;&nbsp;The determination of an adequate allowance is inherently subjective, as it requires estimates that are susceptible to significant revision as additional information becomes available or circumstances change.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The allowance for loan losses consists of a specific and a general allowance component.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The specific component provides for estimated probable losses for loans identified as impaired.&nbsp;&nbsp;A loan is considered impaired when, based on current information and events, it is probable that the Bank will be unable to collect all amounts of principal and interest when due according to the contractual terms of the loan agreement.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management considers the borrower&#x2019;s financial condition, payment status, historical payment record and any adverse situations affecting the borrower&#x2019;s ability to repay when evaluating whether a loan is deemed impaired.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans that experience insignificant payment delays and shortfalls generally are not classified as impaired. Management determines the significance of payment delays and shortfalls on a case-by-case basis taking into consideration all circumstances surrounding the loan and the borrower, including the length of delay, the reasons for the delay, the borrower&#x2019;s prior payment record and the amount of shortfall in relation to the principal and interest outstanding.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">A specific reserve is recorded when and to the extent (i) the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the loan&#x2019;s original effective rate, (ii) the fair value of collateral if the loan is collateral-dependent or (iii) the observable market price of the impaired loan is lower than its recorded investment.&nbsp;&nbsp;If the fair value of collateral is used to measure impairment of a collateral-dependent loan and repayment is dependent on the sale of the collateral, the fair value is adjusted to incorporate estimated costs to sell.&nbsp;&nbsp;Impaired loans that are collateral-dependent are primarily measured for impairment using the fair value of the collateral as determined by third party appraisals using the income approach, recent comparable sales data or a combination thereof.&nbsp;&nbsp;In certain instances it is necessary for management to adjust the appraised value, less estimated costs to sell, to reflect changes in fair value occurring subsequent to the appraisal date.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management considers a guarantor&#x2019;s capacity and willingness to perform, when appropriate, and the borrower&#x2019;s resources available for repayment when measuring impairment.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The general allowance provides for estimated and probable losses inherent in the remainder of the Bank&#x2019;s loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;The general allowance is determined through a statistical calculation based on the Bank's historical loss experience adjusted for certain qualitative factors as deemed appropriate by management.&nbsp;&nbsp;The statistical calculation is conducted on a disaggregated basis for groups of homogeneous loans with similar risk characteristics (product types).&nbsp;&nbsp;The historical loss element is calculated as the average ratio of charge-offs, net of recoveries, to the average recorded investment for the current and previous five quarters.&nbsp;&nbsp;See </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Note 5</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> in the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2013, June 29, 2012 and June 24, 2011 included under Item 8. &#x201C;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data&#x201D; for additional information concerning the historical loss element of the general component of the allowance for loan losses.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management adjusts the historical loss rates to reflect deterioration in the real estate market, significant concentrations of product types and trends in portfolio volume to capture additional risk of loss associated with concentrations of criticized and classified loans in the total loan </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 10pt">

			<font style="display: inline;">-</font><font style="display: inline;">49</font><font style="display: inline;">-</font>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div><hr size="3" style="color:#999999" width="100%" align="center"></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 8pt">

			<a href="#IndexToAnnualReport"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:8pt;">Table Of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Prevailing economic conditions and specific industry trends are taken into consideration when establishing the adjustments to historical loss rates.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Certain types of loans, such as option adjustable rate mortgage (&#x201C;ARM&#x201D;) products, junior lien mortgages, high loan-to-value ratio mortgages, single family interest only loans, sub-prime loans, and loans with initial "teaser" rates, can have a greater risk of non-collection than other loans.&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, the Bank had $8.6 million in junior lien mortgages. These loans represented less than 2% of the Bank&#x2019;s total loans at June 30, 2013.&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, the Bank did not have any exposure to sub-prime loans or loans with initial teaser rates and had no single family interest only loans.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">At June 30, 2013, the Bank&#x2019;s loan portfolio included a total of $1.1 million in loans with high loan-to-value ratios.&nbsp;&nbsp;High loan-to-value ratios are defined by regulation and range from 75%-90% depending on the type of loan.&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, all of these loans were 1-4 single family or lot loans to home builders in North Texas.&nbsp;&nbsp;We addressed the additional risk in these loans in our allowance calculation primarily through our review of the real estate market deterioration adjustment to the historical loss ratio. Additionally, at June 30, 2013, the Bank had no loans with a high loan-to-value ratio that were deemed impaired.&nbsp;&nbsp;Regulatory guidelines suggest that high loan-to-value ratio loans should not exceed 100% of total capital.&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, the Bank&#x2019;s high loan-to-value ratio loans represented less than 1% of total capital.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We obtain appraisals on real estate loans at the time of origination from third party appraisers approved by the Bank&#x2019;s Board of Directors. We may also obtain additional appraisals when the borrower&#x2019;s performance indicates it may default.&nbsp;&nbsp;After a loan default and foreclosure, we obtain new appraisals to determine the fair value of the foreclosed asset. We obtain updated appraisals on foreclosed properties on an annual basis, or more frequently if required by market conditions, until we sell the property.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Management reviews the loan loss computation methodology on a quarterly basis to determine if the factors used in the calculation are appropriate. In the past four years, because our problem loans and losses were concentrated in real estate related loans, we paid particular attention to real estate market deterioration and the concentration of capital in our real estate related loans. Improvement or additional deterioration in the residential and commercial real estate market may have an impact on these factors in future quarters. To the extent we underestimate the impact of these risks, our allowance for loan losses could be materially understated.</font><font style="display: inline;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6pt;text-indent:10.5pt;text-align:left;font-family:Times New Roman;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Loans receivable, including loans measured at fair value, at June 30, 2013, 2012, 2011, 2010 and 2009 are summarized as follows (in thousands):</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-size:8pt;">(*)&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:8pt;">There is no allowance for probable loan loss for loans measured at fair value or purchased mortgage loans held for investment.&nbsp;&nbsp;Purchase mortgage loans held for investment are held on average for 25 days or less, substantially reducing credit risk.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The decrease in purchased mortgage loans held for investment from June 30, 2012 to June 30, 2013 was representative of an overall decline in the first quarter of calendar 2013 in the mortgage industry&#x2019;s production levels.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The nature of purchased mortgage loans held for investment business is volatile and subject to significant variation depending on interest rates, competition and general economic conditions.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We maintain an internally classified loan list that helps us assess the overall quality of the loan portfolio and the adequacy of the allowance for loan losses.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans on this list are classified as substandard, doubtful or loss based on probability of repayment, collateral valuation and related collectability.&nbsp;&nbsp;This list is used to identify loans that are considered non-performing.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We classify loans as non-performing when they are 90 days or more past due as to principal or interest or when reasonable doubt exists as to timely collectability.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank uses a standardized review process to determine which non-performing loans should be placed on non-accrual status.&nbsp;&nbsp;At the time a loan is placed on non-accrual status, we reverse previously accrued and uncollected interest against interest income.&nbsp;&nbsp;We recognize interest income on non-accrual loans to the extent we receive cash payments for the loans with respect to which ultimate full collection is likely.&nbsp;&nbsp;For loans where full collection is not likely, we apply interest payments to the outstanding principal and we recognize income only if full payment is made.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Approximately $1.0 million, $1.1 million and $2.2 million of gross interest income would have been recorded in fiscal 2013, 2012 and 2011, respectively, had the non-accrual loans been recorded in accordance with their original terms.&nbsp;&nbsp;Interest income recorded on the non-accrual loans, prior to being placed on non-accrual status, in fiscal 2013, 2012 and 2011 totaled approximately $0.3 million, $1.2 million and $1.2 million, respectively.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">In fiscal 2011, the Bank hired additional staff and allocated additional resources to manage the growth in REO and non-performing assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;To reduce these loans and properties expeditiously, management prepared an asset-by-asset plan for these asset categories.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management&#x2019;s focus on the continued reduction of these asset classes may have a material impact on the Bank&#x2019;s future results of operations.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Total classified assets to Bank capital plus allowance for loan loss was 37.4% at June 30, 2013.&nbsp;&nbsp;Classified assets decreased $43.1 million from June 30, 2012 to June 30, 2013 and substantially all classified loans by collateral location are in Texas.&nbsp;&nbsp;Bank management continues to be focused on reducing the classified asset ratio through the disposal of these assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;Depending on the method used, the Bank may be required to record additional write-downs of these assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;While management is diligently working to dispose of these assets quickly, lack of demand for certain property types, length of sales cycle and manpower limitations will impact the time required to ultimately reduce the classified assets to a more acceptable level.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"></font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">With the continued challenging economic environment and persistent high unemployment rates, the Bank frequently reviews and updates its processes and procedures for the extension of credit, allowance for loan loss computation and internal asset review and classification.&nbsp;&nbsp;Recent changes include more stringent underwriting guidelines for loan-to-value ratios, guarantor&#x2019;s financial condition, owner-occupied versus investor loans and speculative versus custom construction.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank currently requires more extensive documentation and data than it did in prior years in order to reclassify existing non-performing loans as performing loans.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank is also updating appraisals more frequently, including for performing loans, to serve as an early indicator of loan deterioration.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">As a result of the current economic environment, the Bank significantly limited the growth of its loan portfolio in fiscal 2011 and 2012 in order to allocate the time, resources and capital necessary to support the existing loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;During fiscal 2013, the Bank reestablished marketing efforts to implement a conservative loan growth plan consistent with its business plan which we believe will enhance our core earnings in future years. </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">At June 30, 2013, approximately 26.7% of the Bank&#x2019;s loan loss allowance was allocated to its commercial real estate loan portfolio while the Bank&#x2019;s commercial real estate loan portfolio represented approximately 34.8% of its total loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;This is down from June 30, 2012 when approximately 47.4% of the Bank&#x2019;s loan loss allowance was allocated to its commercial real estate loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;Even though our concentration in commercial real estate loans has decreased, because commercial real estate loans tend to be individually larger than residential loans, deterioration in this portfolio can lead to volatility in our earnings.&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, the loan loss allowance related to multifamily loans was 28.9% as compared to multifamily loans constituting 16.1% of the Bank&#x2019;s total loan portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;The larger allocation of the allowance to multifamily loans reflects the recent growth in this portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;The loan loss allowance allocated to the multifamily loan portfolio has increased 24% from June 30, 2012 to June 30, 2013.&nbsp;&nbsp;This increase was due to the growth in the multifamily loan portfolio from $20.1 million at June 30, 2012 to $99.8 million at June 30, 2013 and the trend in the historical loss element of the general component of the allowance for loan losses.</font>
		</p>

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Bank&#x2019;s written loan policies address specific underwriting standards for commercial real estate loans.&nbsp;&nbsp;These policies include loan to value requirements, cash flow requirements, acceptable amortization periods and appraisal guidelines.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, specific covenants, unique to each relationship, may be used where deemed appropriate to further protect the lending relationship.&nbsp;&nbsp;Collateral in the commercial real estate portfolio varies from owner-occupied properties to investor properties.&nbsp;&nbsp;We periodically review the portfolio for concentrations by industry as well as geography.&nbsp;&nbsp;All commercial relationships are stress tested at the time of origination and major relationships are then stress tested on an annual basis.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">LIQUIDITY AND CAPITAL RESOURCES </font>

		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Management believes that our current assets and available liquidity are adequate to meet our liquidity needs over the next 12 months.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, our forecast may not prove to be accurate or we may need to raise additional capital.&nbsp;&nbsp;As a result, from time to time, management evaluates various opportunities to supplement the company&#x2019;s sources of liquidity and capital.&nbsp;&nbsp;In fiscal 2012, this evaluation led to us entering into the Credit Agreement with Hilltop and Oak Hill, as discussed below.&nbsp;&nbsp;Should we determine we need to obtain additional debt at SWS Group, we would require regulatory approval and approval from Hilltop and Oak Hill.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Credit Agreement</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">On July 29, 2011, we entered into a Credit Agreement with Hilltop and Oak Hill pursuant to which we obtained a $100.0 million, five year, unsecured loan that accrues interest at a rate of 8% per annum.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, we issued warrants to Hilltop and Oak Hill allowing each to purchase up to 8,695,652 shares of common stock at an exercise price of $5.75 per share (subject to anti-dilution adjustments), representing approximately 17% of the common stock of our company per investor as of July 29, 2011 (assuming the warrants are excercised in full).&nbsp;&nbsp;The Credit Agreement contains restrictions and covenants that we must adhere to as long as the unsecured loan is outstanding.&nbsp;&nbsp;As of June 30, 2013, SWS Group had utilized $70.0 million of the $100.0 million by (i) contributing $20.0 million in capital to the Bank to promote growth in the Bank&#x2019;s loan portfolio, (ii) reducing SWS Group&#x2019;s intercompany payable to Southwest Securities by $20.0 million and (iii) contributing $30.0 million in capital to So</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">uthwest Securities.&nbsp;&nbsp;See </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Note 16</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> in the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2013, June 29, 2012 and June 24, 2011 included under Item 8. &#x201C;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data&#x201D; for additional information concerning this Credit Agreement.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Brokerage</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">A substantial portion of our assets are highly liquid in nature and consist mainly of cash or assets that are readily convertible into cash.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our equity capital, short-term bank borrowings, interest bearing and non-interest bearing client credit balances, correspondent deposits and other payables finance these assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;We maintain an allowance for doubtful accounts that represents amounts that are necessary in the judgment of management to adequately absorb losses from known and inherent risks in receivables from clients, clients of correspondents and correspondents. The highly liquid nature of our assets provides us with flexibility in financing and managing our anticipated operating needs.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management believes that the brokerage business' present liquidity position is adequate to meet its needs over the next 12 months.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Banking </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Liquidity is monitored daily to ensure the Bank&#x2019;s ability to meet deposit withdrawals, maintain reserve requirements and otherwise sustain operations.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank&#x2019;s liquidity is maintained in the form of readily marketable loans and investment securities, balances with the FHLB, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, federal funds sold to correspondent banks and vault cash.&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, the Bank had net borrowing capacity from the FHLB of $83.2 million.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, at June 30, 2013, the Bank had the ability to borrow up to $28.3 million in funds from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas under its secondary credit program.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The Bank&#x2019;s asset and liability management policy is intended to manage interest rate risk.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank accomplishes this through management of the periodic repricing of its interest-earning assets and its interest-bearing liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Overall interest rate risk is monitored through reports showing both sensitivity ratios, a simulation model, and existing "GAP" data.&nbsp;&nbsp;(See the Bank&#x2019;s GAP analysis in "-Risk Management-Market Risk-Interest Rate Risk-Banking.")&nbsp;&nbsp;At June 30, 2013, $878.4 million of the Bank&#x2019;s deposits were from the brokerage customers of Southwest Securities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Current events in the securities markets could impact the amount of these funds available to the Bank.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Inflation</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:normal;font-size:9pt;">Our financial statements included herein have been prepared in accordance with GAAP.&nbsp;&nbsp;GAAP requires us to measure our financial position and operating results primarily in terms of historic dollars.&nbsp;&nbsp;Changes in the relative value of money due to inflation or recession are generally not considered under GAAP.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our assets are primarily monetary, consisting of cash, securities inventory and receivables from customers and broker/dealers.&nbsp;&nbsp;These monetary assets are generally liquid and turn over rapidly and, consequently, are not significantly affected by inflation.&nbsp;&nbsp;The rate of inflation affects various expenses of the company, such as employee compensation and benefits, communications, and occupancy and equipment, which may not be readily recoverable in the price of our services.&nbsp;&nbsp;The rate of inflation can also have a significant impact on securities prices and on investment preferences by our customers, generally.&nbsp;&nbsp;In management&#x2019;s opinion, changes in interest rates affect the financial condition of a financial services firm to a greater degree than changes in the inflation rate.&nbsp;&nbsp;While interest rates are greatly influenced by changes in the inflation rate, they do not necessarily change at the same rate or in the same magnitude as the inflation rate.&nbsp;&nbsp;Interest rates are highly sensitive to many factors that are beyond our control, including changes in the expected rate of inflation, the influence of general and local economic conditions and the monetary and fiscal policies of the United States government, its agencies and various other governmental regulatory authorities among other things.&nbsp;&nbsp;See Item 1A, &#x201C;Risk Factors - Risks Specific to Our Industries.&#x201D;</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">RISK M</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">ANAGEMENT</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">In an effort to assist the company in managing enterprise risk, in 2010 and at the Board of Director&#x2019;s request, the company engaged a firm to perform an analysis of the company&#x2019;s enterprise risk management process.&nbsp;&nbsp;During fiscal 2011, based on the Board of Director&#x2019;s recommendations, we initiated an enterprise risk management program and formed a committee.&nbsp;&nbsp;Enterprise risk is viewed as the threat from an event, action of loss of opportunity that, if it occurs or has occurred, may adversely affect any, or any combination of, our company objectives, business strategies, business model, regulatory compliance, reputation and existence.&nbsp;&nbsp;The committee works with our various departments and committees to manage our enterprise risk management program and reports the results of this work to the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors on a quarterly basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;During fiscal 2013, we hired a full time risk manager for the consolidated group who serves as the primary liaison with our risk management consultants.&nbsp;&nbsp;We continue to utilize the consultants to improve risk management processes, procedures and reporting.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We manage risk exposure through the involvement of various levels of management.&nbsp;&nbsp;We establish, maintain and regularly monitor maximum positions by industry and issuer in both trading and inventory accounts.&nbsp;&nbsp;Current and proposed underwriting, banking and other commitments are subject to due diligence reviews by senior management, as well as professionals in the appropriate business and support units.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank seeks to reduce the risk of significant adverse effects of market rate fluctuations by minimizing the difference between rate-sensitive assets and liabilities, referred to as "GAP," and maintaining an interest rate sensitivity position within a particular timeframe.&nbsp;&nbsp;Credit risk related to various financing activities is reduced by the industry practice of obtaining and maintaining collateral.&nbsp;&nbsp;We monitor our exposure to counterparty risk through the use of credit information, the monitoring of collateral values and the establishment of credit limits.&nbsp;&nbsp;We have established various risk management committees that are responsible for reviewing and managing risk related to interest rates, trading positions, margin and other credit risk and risks from capital market transactions.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Credit Risk</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">A description of the credit risk for our brokerage and banking segments is as follows: </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Brokerage</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Credit risk arises from the potential nonperformance by counterparties, customers or debt security issuers.&nbsp;&nbsp;We are exposed to credit risk as a trading counterparty and as a stock loan counterparty to dealers and customers, as a holder of securities and as a member of clearing organizations.&nbsp;&nbsp;We have established credit risk committees to review our credit exposure in our various business units.&nbsp;&nbsp;These committees are composed of senior management of the company.&nbsp;&nbsp;Credit exposure is also associated with customer margin accounts, which are monitored daily.&nbsp;&nbsp;We monitor exposure to individual securities and perform sensitivity analysis on a regular basis in connection with our margin lending activities.&nbsp;&nbsp;We adjust our margin requirements if we believe our risk exposure is not appropriate based on market conditions.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Banking</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Credit risk is the possibility that a borrower or counterparty will fail to meet its obligations in accordance with agreed terms and is inherent in all types of lending.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank has developed and continues to enhance its policies and procedures to provide a process for managing credit risk.&nbsp;&nbsp;These policies and procedures include underwriting guidelines, credit and collateral tracking and detailed loan approval procedures which include officer and director loan committees. The Bank also maintains a detailed loan review process to monitor the quality of its loan portfolio. The Bank makes loans to customers primarily within Texas and New Mexico.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank also purchases mortgage loans, which have been originated in other areas of the United States.&nbsp;&nbsp;Although the Bank has a diversified loan portfolio, a substantial portion of its portfolio is dependent upon the general economic conditions in Texas and New Mexico. Policies and procedures, which are in place to manage credit risk, are designed to be responsive to changes in these economic conditions.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Operational Risk</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Operational risk refers generally to risk of loss resulting from our operations, including but not limited to, improper or unauthorized execution and processing of transactions, deficiencies in our operating systems, and inadequacies or breaches in our control processes.&nbsp;&nbsp;We operate in diverse markets and rely on the ability of our employees and systems to process large numbers of transactions.&nbsp;&nbsp;In order to mitigate and control operational risk, we have developed and continue to enhance specific policies and procedures that are designed to identify and manage operational risk at appropriate levels.&nbsp;&nbsp;We also use periodic self-assessments and internal audit examinations as further review of the effectiveness of our controls and procedures in mitigating our operational risk.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;;font-size: 9pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:normal;font-size:9pt;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Legal Risk&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-align:left;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Legal risk includes the risk of non-compliance with applicable legal and regulatory requirements.&nbsp;&nbsp;We are subject to extensive regulation in the different jurisdictions in which we conduct business.&nbsp;&nbsp;We have established procedures based on legal and regulatory requirements that are designed to reasonably ensure compliance with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements.&nbsp;&nbsp;We also have established procedures that are designed to ensure that executive management&#x2019;s policies relating to conduct, ethics and business practices are followed.&nbsp;&nbsp;In connection with our business, we have various procedures addressing significant issues such as regulatory capital requirements, sales and trading practices, new products, use and safekeeping of customer funds and securities, granting credit, collection activities, money laundering, privacy and record keeping.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Market Risk&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-align:left;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Market risk generally represents the risk of loss that may result from the potential change in value of a financial instrument as a result of fluctuations in interest rates, market prices, investor expectations and changes in credit ratings of the issuer.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our exposure to market risk is directly related to our role as a financial intermediary in customer-related transactions and to our proprietary trading activities and securities lending activities. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:0pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Interest Rate Risk.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> A description of the interest rate risk for our brokerage and banking segments is as follows:</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Brokerage</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Interest rate risk is a consequence of maintaining inventory positions and trading in interest rate sensitive financial instruments and maintaining a matched stock loan book.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our fixed income activities also expose us to the risk of loss related to changes in credit spreads.&nbsp;&nbsp;Credit spread risk arises from the potential that changes in an issuer&#x2019;s credit rating or credit perception could affect the value of financial instruments.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 9pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Banking</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our primary emphasis in interest rate risk management for the Bank is the matching of assets and liabilities of similar cash flow and re-pricing time frames.&nbsp;&nbsp;This matching of assets and liabilities reduces exposure to interest rate movements and aids in stabilizing positive interest spreads.&nbsp;&nbsp;We strive to structure our balance sheet as a natural hedge by matching floating rate assets with variable short term funding and by matching fixed rate liabilities with similar longer term fixed rate assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Bank has established percentage change limits in both interest margin and net portfolio value.&nbsp; To verify that the Bank is within the limits established for interest margin, the Bank prepares an analysis&nbsp;of net interest margin based on various shifts in interest rates.&nbsp;&nbsp;To verify that the Bank is within the limits established for net portfolio value, the Bank analyzes data prepared using internal modeling data for net portfolio value.&nbsp;&nbsp;These analyses are conducted on a quarterly basis for the Bank&#x2019;s Board of Directors.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The following table illustrates the estimated change in net interest margin based on shifts in interest rates of positive 300 basis points to negative 100 basis points:</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">CRITICAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES AND ESTIMATES </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Our discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations are based on our consolidated financial statements, which have been prepared in accordance with GAAP. The preparation of these consolidated financial statements requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses and related disclosures.&nbsp;&nbsp;We review our estimates on an on-going basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;We base our estimates on our experience and on various other assumptions that we believe to be reasonable under the circumstances.&nbsp;&nbsp;Actual results may differ from these estimates under different assumptions or conditions.&nbsp;&nbsp;The following policies involve a higher degree of judgment than do our other significant accounting policies detailed in </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Note 1</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> in the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2013, June 29, 2012 and June 24, 2011 included under Item 8. &#x201C;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data.&#x201D;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Fair Value</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We adopted the fair value accounting standard of the FASB effective June 28, 2008.&nbsp;&nbsp;Fair value accounting establishes a framework for measuring fair value and expands disclosures about fair value measurements.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Under fair value accounting, fair value refers to the price that would be received upon the sale ofan asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants in the principal market in which the reporting entity transacts.&nbsp;&nbsp;The standard clarifies the principle that fair value should be based on the assumptions market participants would use</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">when pricing the asset or liability.&nbsp;&nbsp;In support of this principle, the standard establishes a fair value hierarchy that prioritizes the information used to develop those assumptions.&nbsp;&nbsp;The fair value hierarchy gives the highest priority to quoted prices in active markets and the lowest priority to unobservable data.&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the standard, fair value measurements are separately disclosed by level within the fair value hierarchy.&nbsp;&nbsp;The standard describes three levels of inputs that may be used to measure fair value:&nbsp; </font>
		</p>

						<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Level&nbsp;2&nbsp;&#x2014; Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities; quoted prices in markets that are not active; or other inputs that are observable or can be corroborated by observable market data for substantially the full term of the assets or liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;We value the following assets and liabilities utilizing Level&nbsp;2 inputs:&nbsp;&nbsp;(i) the Bank&#x2019;s loans measured at fair value;&nbsp;&nbsp;(ii) the Bank&#x2019;s investment in interest rate swaps; (iii) certain inventories held in our securities owned and securities sold, not yet purchased portfolio and (iv) securities in our available for sale portfolio.&nbsp;&nbsp;These financial instruments are valued by quoted prices that are less frequent than those in active markets or by models that use various assumptions that are derived from or supported by data that is generally observable in the marketplace. Valuations in this category are inherently less reliable than quoted market prices due to the degree of subjectivity involved in determining appropriate methodologies and the applicable observable market underlying assumptions.&nbsp; </font></p>

						<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Level&nbsp;3&nbsp;&#x2014; Unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and that are significant to the fair value of the assets and liabilities.&nbsp;&nbsp;We value the following assets and liabilities utilizing Level 3 inputs:&nbsp;&nbsp;(i) certain inventories held in our securities owned portfolio and (ii) the warrants issued to Hilltop and Oak Hill. These financial instruments have significant inputs that cannot be validated by readily determinable market data and generally involve considerable judgment by management.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our Level 3 assets represented less than 1% of our total assets measured at fair value at June 30, 2013.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our Level 3 liabilities represented 15% of our total liabilities measured at fair value at June 30, 2013.&nbsp;&nbsp;All of our Level 3 liabilities consist of the warrants issued to Hilltop and Oak Hill.</font></p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The availability of observable inputs can vary for different assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;Fair value is a market-based measure; therefore, when market observable inputs are not available, our judgment is applied to reflect those judgments that we believe a market participant would use in valuing the same asset or liability.&nbsp;&nbsp;We use prices and inputs that are current as of the measurement date even in periods of market disruption or illiquidity.&nbsp;&nbsp;Greater judgment in valuation is required when inputs are less observable or unobservable in the marketplace and judgment must be applied in determining the appropriateness of available prices, particularly in assessing whether available data reflects current prices and/or reflects the results of recent market transactions.&nbsp;&nbsp;The valuation of financial instruments classified in Level 3 of the fair value hierarchy involves the greatest amount of management judgment.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent: -36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;text-decoration:underline;">Valuation Process for Financial Instruments.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;Financial instruments are valued at quoted market prices, if available.&nbsp;&nbsp;For financial instruments that do not have readily determinable fair values through quoted market prices, the determination of fair value is based upon consideration of available information including current financial information, fair values of underlying financial instruments and quotations for similar instruments.&nbsp;&nbsp;Certain financial instruments have bid and ask prices that can be observed in the marketplace.&nbsp;&nbsp;For financial instruments whose inputs are based on bid-ask prices, mid-market pricing is applied and adjusted to the point within the bid-ask range that meets our best estimate of fair value.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent: -36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The valuation process for financial instruments may include the use of valuation models and other techniques.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management makes adjustments to valuations derived from valuation models based on a number of factors, including but not limited to, the size of the position in the financial instrument in an inactive market, the features of the financial instrument such as its complexity, the market in which the financial instrument is traded or if a financial instrument is subject to sales restrictions that would result in a price less than the quoted market price.&nbsp;&nbsp;Adjustments from the price derived from a valuation model reflect management&#x2019;s judgment that other participants in the market for the financial instrument would consider the same factors in valuing the financial instrument.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Management makes assumptions about risk, uncertainties and market conditions in preparing adjustments to prices derived from a valuation model.&nbsp;&nbsp;Results from valuation models and valuation techniques in one period may not be indicative of future period fair value measurements.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;text-indent: -36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Certain financial instruments and other assets trade infrequently and therefore have outdated market prices.&nbsp;&nbsp;As a result, we may use alternative valuation models as methods for determining fair value of these assets.&nbsp;&nbsp;When using alternative valuation techniques or valuation models, the following techniques are applied to different financial instrument classes:</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt 5pt 36pt;text-indent: -13.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&#x25CF;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:6pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Non-agency mortgage-backed and other asset-backed securities are valued by benchmarking to yields from market prices for comparable securities and calibrated based on expected cash flow characteristics of the underlying assets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The following is a description of the valuation methodologies used for instruments measured at fair value on a recurring basis and recognized in the accompanying statement of financial condition, as well as the general classification of such instruments pursuant to the valuation hierarchy.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 22.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Loans measured at fair value.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The fair value of loans for which the fair value option has been elected is calculated based on the present value of expected future discounted cash flows using market interest rates currently being offered for loans with similar terms to borrowers with comparable credit risk.&nbsp;&nbsp;These loans are classified as Level 2.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 22.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt 5pt 22.3pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Securities Available for Sale</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Because quoted market prices are available in an active market, our deferred compensation plan&#x2019;s investment in Westwood&#x2019;s common stock is classified within Level 1 of the valuation hierarchy.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our investments in U.S. government and government agency obligations and municipal obligations held by the Bank as available for sale are valued in a similar manner to our Level 2 securities owned and securities sold, not yet purchased portfolio, noted below. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 22.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 22.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 9pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Securities Owned and Securities Sold, Not Yet Purchased Portfolio</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Securities classified as Level 1 securities primarily consist of financial instruments whose values are based on quoted market prices such as corporate equity securities and U.S. government and government agency obligations, primarily U.S. treasury securities.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 24.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;line-height:normal;text-indent: -24.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 22.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Securities classified as Level 2 securities include financial instruments that are valued using models or other valuation methodologies.&nbsp;&nbsp;These models are primarily industry standard models that consider various assumptions, including time value, yield curve, volatility factors, current market and contractual prices for the underlying financial instruments, as well as other relevant economic measures.&nbsp;&nbsp;Substantially all of these assumptions are observable in the marketplace, can be derived from observable data or are supported by observable levels at which transactions are executed in the marketplace.&nbsp;&nbsp;Securities in this category include corporate obligations, U.S. government and government agency obligations and municipal obligations.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 24.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 22.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Securities classified as Level 3 securities are securities whose fair values are estimated based on internally developed models or methodologies, including discounted cash flow, utilizing significant inputs that are generally less readily observable.&nbsp;&nbsp;The models and methodologies considered the quality of the underlying loans, any related secondary market activity and expectations regarding future interest rate movements.&nbsp;&nbsp;Included in this category are certain corporate equity securities and corporate obligations.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 18pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0pt 22.5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Interest rate swaps.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;Interest rate swaps </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">are valued </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">using an income approach incorporating various assumptions, including the term of the swap, the notional amount of the swap, discount rates interpolated based on relevant swap curves, the rate on the fixed leg of the swap and a credit value adjustment for counterparty non-performance.&nbsp;&nbsp;The approach also takes into consideration the potential impact of collateralization and netting agreements.&nbsp;&nbsp;These interest rate swaps are classified as Level 2</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt 5pt 22.5pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;">Stock purchase warrants.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The warrants held by Hilltop and Oak Hill are valued quarterly using a binomial model.&nbsp;&nbsp;The model considers the following variables: price and volatility of our common stock, treasury yield, annual dividend, and the remaining life of the warrants.&nbsp;&nbsp;The derived volatility estimate considers both the historical and implied forward volatility of our common stock.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;All else being equal, the warrants will lose time value as they near maturity.&nbsp;&nbsp;Other than remaining life, the primary drivers of value are the price and volatility of our common stock.&nbsp;&nbsp;As the volatility and/or stock price increase, the value of the warrants increase as well.&nbsp;&nbsp;The movement of these two variables will amplify or offset one another depending on the direction and velocity of their movements.&nbsp;&nbsp;These securities are classified as Level 3.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Contingencies</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Accounting for contingencies requires the use of judgment and estimates in assessing the magnitude of the exposure and the likely outcome of the situation.&nbsp;&nbsp;In many cases, the outcome will be determined by third parties, which may include governmental or judicial bodies.&nbsp;&nbsp;The provisions made in our consolidated financial statements, as well as the related disclosures, represent management&#x2019;s best estimates of the current status of such matters and their potential outcome based on a review of the facts and, when warranted, in consultation with outside legal counsel.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management evaluates and revises its estimates on a quarterly basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Adverse legal or arbitration judgments, inability to collect receivables, sudden declines in the fair value of securities held in margin accounts or other actions could result in material changes to the estimates recorded in these financial statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;Resolution of these matters in amounts different from what has been accrued in the consolidated financial statements could materially impact our financial position and results of operations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Long-Lived Assets and Goodwill&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-align:left;text-indent:36pt;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Our long-lived assets are subject to impairment testing if specific events warrant the review.&nbsp;&nbsp;We test goodwill for impairment at least annually.&nbsp;&nbsp;The impairment test is based on determining the fair value of the specified reporting units.&nbsp;&nbsp;Judgment is required in assessing the effects of external factors, including market conditions, and projecting future operating results.&nbsp;&nbsp;These judgments and assumptions could materially change the value of the specified reporting units and, therefore, could materially impact our consolidated financial statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;If actual external conditions and future operating results differ from management&#x2019;s judgments, impairment charges may be necessary to reduce the carrying value of these assets to the appropriate fair value.&nbsp;&nbsp;See additional discussion in </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Note 1(k)</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> in the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2013, June 29, 2012 and June 24, 2011 included under Item 8. &#x201C;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data&#x201D;.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Allowance for Probable Loan Losses&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We provide an allowance for probable loan losses.&nbsp;&nbsp;The allowance for loan losses is established as losses are estimated to have occurred through a provision for loan losses charged to earnings.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loan losses are charged against the allowance when management believes the uncollectability of a loan balance is confirmed.&nbsp;&nbsp;Subsequent recoveries, if any, are credited to the </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 10pt">

			<font style="display: inline;">-</font><font style="display: inline;">65</font><font style="display: inline;">-</font>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div><hr size="3" style="color:#999999" width="100%" align="center"></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 8pt">

			<a href="#IndexToAnnualReport"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:8pt;">Table Of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-size: 10pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">allowance.&nbsp;&nbsp;Should actual losses differ from management&#x2019;s estimates, our consolidated financial statements could be materially impacted.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The allowance for loan losses is evaluated on a regular basis by management and is based upon management&#x2019;s periodic review of the collectability of the loans in light of historical experience, the nature and volume of the loan portfolio, adverse situations that may affect the borrower&#x2019;s ability to repay, estimated value of any underlying collateral and prevailing economic conditions.&nbsp;&nbsp;This evaluation is inherently subjective, as it requires estimates that are susceptible to significant revision as more information becomes available.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">The allowance consists of specific and general components.&nbsp;&nbsp;The specific component relates to loans that are classified as doubtful, substandard or special mention.&nbsp;&nbsp;For such loans that are also classified as impaired, an allowance is established when the collateral value (or discounted cash flows or observable market price) of the impaired loan is lower than the carrying value of that loan.&nbsp;&nbsp;The general component covers all loans and is based on historical loss experience adjusted for qualitative factors.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;&nbsp;These factors include the following: concentrations of risk in the portfolio, estimated changes in the value of underlying collateral, and changes in the volume and growth in the portfolio</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">. &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Impaired loans are accounted for at the fair value of the collateral if the loan is collateral dependent, the net present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the loan&#x2019;s effective interest rate or at the observable market price of the loan.</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> &nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">A loan is considered impaired when, based on current information and events, it is probable that the Bank will be unable to collect the scheduled payments of principal or interest when due according to the contractual terms of the loan agreement.&nbsp;&nbsp;Factors considered by management in determining impairment include payment status, collateral value, and the probability of collecting scheduled principal and interest payments when due.&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans that experience insignificant payment delays and payment shortfalls generally are not classified as impaired.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management determines the significance of payment delays and payment shortfalls on a case-by-case basis, taking into consideration all of the circumstances surrounding the loan and the borrower, including the length of the delay, the reasons for the delay, the borrower&#x2019;s prior payment record, and the amount of the shortfall in relation to the principal and interest owed.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:CG Times (W1);font-weight:bold;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Income Tax Accrual and Allowance for Deferred Tax Assets&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6pt;text-indent:10.5pt;text-align:left;font-family:Times New Roman;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We operate in multiple taxing jurisdictions, and as a result, accruals for tax contingencies require us to make estimates and judgments with respect to the ultimate tax liability in any given fiscal year.&nbsp;&nbsp;Actual results could vary from these estimates.&nbsp;&nbsp;Changes in tax laws, new tax rulings, or results of tax audits could cause management&#x2019;s estimates to change.&nbsp;&nbsp;In our opinion, adequate provisions for income taxes have been made for all fiscal years.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">We record net deferred tax assets to the extent management believes these assets are more likely than not to be realized.&nbsp;&nbsp;In making such determination, management considers all available positive and negative evidence, including: expected future reversals of deferred tax assets and liabilities, projected future taxable income, cumulative losses in recent years and tax planning strategies and recent financial operations.&nbsp;&nbsp;A valuation allowance is established against deferred tax assets when management determines that these deferred assets are more likely to not be realized.&nbsp;&nbsp;In the event management subsequently determines that we would be able to realize deferred income tax assets in excess of their net recorded amount, we would reduce the valuation allowance, which would reduce the provision for income taxes.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:36pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Deferred tax assets derived from operating losses are realized when we generate consolidated taxable income within the applicable carry-back and carry-forward periods.&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on an evaluation of the positive and negative evidence, management determined that a $30.9 million valuation allowance for our deferred tax assets as of June 30, 2013 was appropriate.&nbsp;&nbsp;See </font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-weight:bold;font-size:9pt;">Note 17</font><font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;"> in the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2013, june 29, 2012 and June 24, 2011 included under Item 8. &#x201C;Financial Statements and Supplementary Data&#x201D; for additional detail regarding the Company&#x2019;s deferred tax assets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:5pt 0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Century Schoolbook;font-size:9pt;">Changes in Internal Control Over Financial Reporting.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;text-indent:36pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 9pt">
